newsitem.title: USA: Holiday shoppers to spend 20 pct more on gifts.
newsitem.headline: Holiday shoppers to spend 20 pct more on gifts.

text.p: Consumers will open their wallets a little wider this holiday season by spending about 20 percent more on gifts than last year, a survey said Thursday.

Shoppers' spirits are higher this season due to the buoyant economy and the presidential election, according to a poll by the Gallup Organisation, Visa and the International Mass Retail Association, a trade group. On average, consumers are expected to spend $806 on holiday presents, versus $655 in 1995.
"We see consumers did indicate they will be spending a few extra dollars on their holiday purchases this year," Debra Christenson, a Gallup analyst, told a press conference in New York.

The forecast stems from a poll of 1,009 consumers with a mean income of $32,730. The results were more promising for retailers than a separate survey released last week by another trade group that forecast a 12 percent increase in holiday spending to $764 a consumer.

Still, not all consumers are budgeting so generously. The Gallup survey showed that consumers earning less than $20,000 will fork out $444 on average for holiday presents while those earning $50,000 or more will spend $1,118 on average.

The number of consumers who plan to spend more this holiday season is up only slightly from a year ago. This year, 13 percent of consumers said they would budget more for gifts, compared with 12 percent in 1995 and 17 percent in 1994.

The survey comes on the same day that retailers reported modest increases in retail sales for the month of October. A Salomon Brothers index of same-store sales showed growth of 4.8 percent in October, up from 0.4 percent a year ago and 3.7 percent in September of 1996.

Retailers are generally more optimistic this year about Christmas sales because of positive consumer confidence readings and strong housing start figures, Gallup said. In addition, many stores are more prepared to combat price wars by stocking less merchandise than last year.
"We're in a very highly promotional environment right now," said Joseph Ettore, president and chief executive of Ames Department Stores Inc.
"In the Northeast, with the condition of certain regional discounters, it becomes even more promotional because of their efforts to get back on track with sales," he added.

Last year, a wave of store closings and going-out-of business sales by weak and bankrupt retailers forced all stores to mark down merchandise to draw customers. But this year, retailers have kept inventories lean, which should result in fewer clearance sales after Christmas.

Some experts worry that the compressed holiday shopping season, with five fewer days between Thanksgiving and Christmas this year, will spur chains to start discounting goods the minute customer traffic slows in December.
But Ronald Hudgens, a vice president of merchandising at Kmart Corp., said the discount giant expects customers to buy just as many gifts as usual despite the shorter season.
"We feel the customer will still spend the same amount in fewer days," he said.
